tracks.title: Foundations
tracks.description: Core investigative reasoning, evidence principles, bias control, scene context, and reporting doctrine. All lessons are visible and accessible.

modules.title: Investigative Thinking Frameworks
modules.summary: Build disciplined inference habits: hypotheses, falsification, uncertainty handling, and reasoning hygiene.

lessons.title: What Is Investigative Reasoning?
lessons.objective: Define investigative reasoning as structured inference under uncertainty and distinguish it from narrative-driven thinking.

blocks.content: Investigative reasoning is the disciplined process of forming conclusions from incomplete, evolving, and sometimes conflicting information. It requires documented assumptions, competing hypotheses, and continuous revision as new evidence arrives.
Write one early assumption investigators commonly make and one method to challenge it before it hardens into a narrative.

lessons.title: Hypothesis Generation: Always Hold Multiple
lessons.objective: Practice generating multiple plausible explanations and defining what evidence would falsify each.

blocks.content: A single-theory approach invites confirmation bias. Instead, generate at least three plausible explanations, identify discriminating evidence, and sequence collection steps to reduce ambiguity quickly.
A person disappears after being seen at a transit station. Create three hypotheses before viewing CCTV and list one falsifier for each.
Which hypothesis is most tempting and why? What would keep you from overcommitting to it?

lessons.title: Evidence vs Interpretation
lessons.objective: Separate raw observations from inferred meaning to reduce narrative contamination.

blocks.content: Evidence is what can be observed, measured, recorded, or reliably reported. Interpretation is meaning assigned to evidence. Investigations fail when interpretation is treated as if it were evidence.

items: Required bridge: 'Validate timeframe, access, and alternative explanations.'

blocks.content: Provide two examples from any case type where interpretation can outpace evidence.

lessons.title: Falsification Thinking
lessons.objective: Adopt falsification as a default method for hypothesis testing.

blocks.content: Falsification asks: what would prove my theory wrong? Investigators using falsification seek disconfirming evidence early because it prevents wasted time and reduces bias.

items: Track why a hypothesis was rejected.

blocks.content: Pick one hypothesis from a recent investigation scenario and list two strong falsifiers.

lessons.title: Uncertainty and Confidence Discipline
lessons.objective: Use confidence language that matches evidence quality and avoid certainty inflation.

blocks.content: Investigations operate on probabilities, not certainties. Confidence should reflect source reliability, corroboration, and chain-of-custody integrity. Overconfidence creates brittle conclusions and missed alternatives.
Rewrite a strong claim into calibrated language that accurately reflects uncertainty.

lessons.title: Competing Hypotheses Drill
lessons.objective: Practice ranking hypotheses using discriminating evidence rather than intuition.

blocks.content: A break-in shows forced entry, but nothing valuable is missing. A neighbor reports 'two voices' near the door. Rank three hypotheses and list the top two discriminating tests.
What evidence would most quickly reduce uncertainty in this case?
Which hypothesis is most fragile and why?

lessons.title: Reasoning Hygiene: Notes, Time, and Scope
lessons.objective: Apply reasoning hygiene practices that prevent drift and memory bias.

blocks.content: Reasoning hygiene is a set of habits that keeps investigations coherent: timestamped notes, explicit assumptions, separation of raw facts from inferences, and periodic scope checks.

items: Re-check scope weekly (or per major evidence).

blocks.content: List three fields your investigation notes must always include to stay bias-resistant.

lessons.title: Narrative Contamination Stress Test
lessons.objective: Detect narrative contamination and rebuild conclusions using evidence-first structure.

blocks.content: You are given a one-paragraph narrative summary written by a colleague. Identify which statements are evidence vs interpretation, then rewrite the summary as evidence-first bullet points.
What parts of the narrative were persuasive but unsupported?
What additional evidence would be needed to support the strongest interpretation?

modules.title: Evidence Principles
modules.summary: Evidence hierarchy, reliability, corroboration, chain of custody, and interpretation boundaries.

lessons.title: Evidence Hierarchy
lessons.objective: Explain evidence hierarchy and why higher reliability sources reduce investigative error.

blocks.content: Evidence varies in reliability. Physical records with chain-of-custody are generally stronger than uncorroborated statements. A hierarchy helps prioritize what can anchor conclusions.
Give an example where a low-tier source misled an investigation and how hierarchy would have prevented it.

lessons.title: Corroboration Strategy
lessons.objective: Use corroboration to increase confidence and reduce false positives.

blocks.content: Corroboration is the process of independently confirming an element of evidence. Strong corroboration uses sources that do not share the same failure mode.

items: Corroborate time, place, identity, and mechanism separately.

blocks.content: List two weak corroboration patterns and how to strengthen them.

lessons.title: Chain of Custody: Why It Matters
lessons.objective: Describe chain of custody as a trust system for physical evidence integrity.

blocks.content: Chain of custody documents who collected evidence, when, where it was stored, and who accessed it. Breaks in custody weaken confidence and can invalidate conclusions.
A bag of evidence sits unsealed for 30 minutes after collection. List what conclusions become weaker and what remediation steps are required.
What fields must custody documentation include to remain defensible?

lessons.title: Time Integrity and Evidence Windows
lessons.objective: Use time windows to constrain hypotheses and avoid timeline drift.

blocks.content: Time integrity is the discipline of preserving 'when' across evidence types. Establish windows for events, then use evidence to tighten them. Avoid letting assumptions fill gaps.

items: Separate observed time from estimated time.

blocks.content: Create a time window for a hypothetical event and list two evidence sources that could tighten it.

lessons.title: Evidence Weighting Drill
lessons.objective: Rank evidence items by reliability without using story bias.

blocks.content: You have: one witness statement, a partial CCTV view, a phone location ping, and a recovered item with uncertain custody. Rank them by reliability and explain why.
Which item is most likely to be misinterpreted and how would you guard against that?
What single additional check would raise confidence the most?

lessons.title: Avoiding Overinterpretation
lessons.objective: Identify common overinterpretation traps and use guardrails to prevent them.

blocks.content: Overinterpretation occurs when evidence is stretched beyond what it supports. Guardrails include alternative explanation lists, replication checks, and explicit 'limits' statements in reporting.

items: Prefer conservative conclusions when stakes are high.

blocks.content: Write a 'limits' statement for a piece of ambiguous evidence.

lessons.title: Corroboration Map Lab
lessons.objective: Build a corroboration map that shows independence and failure modes.

blocks.content: Create a map connecting evidence items to the claims they support. Mark which items share origins (same witness group, same device, same collector) and identify single points of failure.
Which claim is supported by the most independent evidence?
Where does your map show fragile support that needs reinforcement?

modules.title: Bias Control and Analytical Discipline
modules.summary: Identify and neutralize cognitive bias patterns that distort investigations.

lessons.title: Confirmation Bias
lessons.objective: Recognize confirmation bias and implement countermeasures.

blocks.content: Confirmation bias is the tendency to seek, interpret, and remember evidence in ways that support an existing belief. In investigations, it appears as selective collection and narrative filtering.
Describe a step in your workflow where confirmation bias is likely and add a countermeasure.

lessons.title: Anchoring and First-Report Bias
lessons.objective: Detect anchoring bias from initial reports and protect later interpretation.

blocks.content: Anchoring occurs when early information disproportionately shapes conclusions. First reports can be wrong yet still define the narrative. Protect analysis by labeling early claims as provisional.
An initial caller claims 'two masked men'. Later CCTV is unclear. Explain how anchoring would distort your search.
What procedural rule would reduce anchoring in your team?

lessons.title: Availability Bias
lessons.objective: Avoid letting vivid recent cases distort current probability estimates.

blocks.content: Availability bias causes people to overestimate likelihood based on recent memorable events. Investigators may see patterns that match the last case instead of the evidence in front of them.

items: Document why a pattern match is justified.

blocks.content: Name one reason a case may feel similar to a previous case but still be fundamentally different.

lessons.title: Outcome Bias
lessons.objective: Evaluate decisions by process quality, not by outcome alone.

blocks.content: Outcome bias judges decisions based on results, ignoring whether the reasoning process was sound. Good processes sometimes produce bad outcomes due to uncertainty.
A correct investigative process leads to a dead end because evidence was destroyed. Describe how to evaluate the team's work fairly.
List two process metrics that matter more than outcome in early-stage investigations.

lessons.title: Premature Closure
lessons.objective: Prevent prematurely ending inquiry when a plausible story appears.

blocks.content: Premature closure is stopping the search once a coherent narrative forms. It is especially common when pressure is high. Counter it with 'closure tests' and red-team questions.

items: Ask: what would change my mind?
Keep at least one alternative alive until key evidence arrives.

blocks.content: Design a closure test checklist for your case type.

lessons.title: Bias Spotting Drill
lessons.objective: Identify bias patterns in short investigative summaries.

blocks.content: Read a short summary and label: anchoring, confirmation, availability, or premature closure. Then rewrite the summary evidence-first.
Which bias was strongest and how did it change the investigation path?
What single sentence would have prevented the bias?

lessons.title: Structured Peer Review
lessons.objective: Use peer review to catch reasoning errors before they compound.

blocks.content: Peer review works best when structured: reviewers ask evidence/assumption questions, request alternative hypotheses, and verify time integrity. It is not a debate—it is a quality gate.
Create a 5-question peer review template for your team.

lessons.title: Red-Team Hypothesis Lab
lessons.objective: Stress test a working theory by constructing the strongest competing explanation.

blocks.content: Take a working hypothesis and build the strongest alternative explanation using the same evidence set. Identify which evidence would discriminate them.
Which single evidence item would most strongly separate the two hypotheses?
What would you change in your evidence collection plan after this lab?

modules.title: Scene Context and Situation Modeling
modules.summary: Model scenes as systems: people, constraints, time windows, and plausible action pathways.

lessons.title: Scene as a System
lessons.objective: Model a scene as interacting components rather than a story backdrop.

blocks.content: A scene is a system: people, objects, constraints, and time. Modeling the system reveals plausible pathways and rules out impossible narratives.
Pick a simple scene and list the top 5 constraints that shape what could have happened.

lessons.title: Access and Opportunity Mapping
lessons.objective: Use access mapping to constrain suspect sets and hypotheses.

blocks.content: Access mapping asks: who could physically or digitally reach the target within the relevant time window? Opportunity is necessary but not sufficient; it narrows search responsibly.
A restricted room shows missing inventory. List access pathways and how to validate each.
What evidence distinguishes 'access' from 'use'?

lessons.title: Pathway Reconstruction
lessons.objective: Reconstruct plausible movement and action pathways without overfitting.

blocks.content: Pathway reconstruction builds plausible action sequences constrained by space, time, and capability. Avoid overfitting: keep multiple pathways until discriminators are found.
Write two different pathways that explain the same evidence set.

lessons.title: Contextual Noise vs Signal
lessons.objective: Separate relevant context from distracting but vivid details.

blocks.content: Scenes contain noise: irrelevant traces, unrelated clutter, and coincidental conditions. Analysts must decide what is signal by testing relevance to hypotheses and time windows.
A scene includes multiple unrelated items. Identify which items are likely noise and which might be signal, and explain your criteria.
What criteria do you use to label something as 'context noise'?

lessons.title: Constraint-First Scene Outline
lessons.objective: Create a constraint-first outline that prevents premature narrative closure.

blocks.content: Outline a scene using only constraints and observations. Then list three hypotheses that fit the constraint model.
Which hypothesis requires the fewest assumptions?
What would falsify the strongest hypothesis?

lessons.title: Time-Place Coupling
lessons.objective: Understand how time and place couple to restrict plausible sequences.

blocks.content: Time-place coupling recognizes that location constraints change over time: doors lock, traffic patterns shift, people rotate, and access changes. Use it to tighten pathways.
Give one example where time-place coupling eliminates a plausible but incorrect hypothesis.

lessons.title: Scene Model Lab
lessons.objective: Build a scene model, then test it against two competing hypotheses.

blocks.content: Create a structured model: constraints, access, time windows, and key observations. Test two hypotheses and note where the model supports or contradicts each.
Which observation is most underexplained and needs targeted collection?
What is the single biggest model assumption you made?

modules.title: Documentation and Reporting Doctrine
modules.summary: Write defensible, evidence-first reports with calibrated confidence and clear limits.

lessons.title: Evidence-First Writing
lessons.objective: Write reports that distinguish facts, inferences, and recommendations.

blocks.content: Evidence-first reporting prevents narrative contamination. Reports should clearly separate raw observations, inferred interpretations, and recommended next actions. This improves auditability and reduces downstream error.
Rewrite one narrative paragraph into evidence-first structure with facts/inferences/limits.

lessons.title: Calibrated Confidence Language
lessons.objective: Use confidence language that matches evidence strength and corroboration.

blocks.content: Calibrated language keeps claims aligned with evidence quality. Avoid absolute statements unless warranted by strong, corroborated, high-integrity evidence.

items: Add explicit limits when evidence is ambiguous.

blocks.content: Convert three absolute statements into calibrated statements with limits.

lessons.title: Assumption Tracking
lessons.objective: Track assumptions explicitly so later evidence can revise them cleanly.

blocks.content: Assumptions should be explicit and reviewable. When assumptions are hidden, they become invisible drivers of bias. Use an 'Assumptions' section with timestamps and revision notes.
Create a 5-line assumption log for a hypothetical case.

lessons.title: Timeline Integrity in Reports
lessons.objective: Prevent timeline drift by documenting time windows and uncertainties.

blocks.content: Timeline integrity requires reporting time as windows, not points, unless directly observed. Always state uncertainty bounds and the evidence supporting them.
You have two timestamps that conflict by 7 minutes. Show how to report this without forcing a false precision.
Write a 'time window' statement with uncertainty and evidence citation.

lessons.title: Report Clarity Drill
lessons.objective: Improve clarity by separating evidence from interpretation and adding limits.

blocks.content: You are given a mixed paragraph combining facts and interpretations. Separate it into three sections: facts, inferences, limits.
What was the most misleading inference and why?
Add one recommended next action that would discriminate competing hypotheses.

lessons.title: Decision Logs and Auditability
lessons.objective: Use decision logs to make investigative choices auditable and reversible.

blocks.content: Decision logs capture why choices were made, what alternatives were considered, and what evidence justified action. This enables review, accountability, and learning.
Design a decision log template with at least 6 fields.

lessons.title: Defensible Summary Lab
lessons.objective: Produce a defensible executive summary that preserves uncertainty and limits.

blocks.content: Write an executive summary from a mixed evidence set. You must include: top facts, top inferences, limits, and next actions. Avoid certainty inflation.
Which inference is strongest? What evidence makes it strong?
Which inference is weakest? What evidence would strengthen it?

modules.title: Ethics and Discipline
modules.summary: Ethical constraints, harm reduction, fairness, and disciplined language in investigative contexts.

lessons.title: Ethical Boundaries in Investigations
lessons.objective: Understand ethical boundaries as constraints that protect integrity and reduce harm.

blocks.content: Ethical boundaries protect investigation integrity and prevent harm. They also preserve evidence admissibility and public trust. Ethical discipline is operational discipline.
List three ethical constraints that should guide evidence collection planning.

lessons.title: Fairness and Bias Avoidance
lessons.objective: Prevent unfair targeting by enforcing evidence-based thresholds for attention.

blocks.content: Fairness requires that investigative attention be evidence-driven. Use objective criteria and corroboration requirements before escalating focus on a person or group.
A tip suggests a suspect based on stereotypes. Describe how to validate claims without bias contamination.
Write one rule that prevents stereotype-driven escalation.

lessons.title: Harm Reduction Thinking
lessons.objective: Apply harm reduction to investigative decisions and communications.

blocks.content: Harm reduction asks how to pursue truth while minimizing unnecessary damage: reputational, psychological, and operational. Good investigators control information release and avoid premature accusations.

items: Use calibrated language in all notes.

blocks.content: Identify one point where communication could cause harm and how to reduce it.

lessons.title: Integrity Under Pressure
lessons.objective: Maintain disciplined reasoning under urgency and external pressure.

blocks.content: Pressure increases the risk of premature closure and biased shortcuts. Integrity under pressure means keeping your method intact: hypotheses, falsifiers, and evidence hierarchy.
A stakeholder demands a fast conclusion. Write a response that preserves method while addressing urgency.
What is your personal trigger for cutting corners and how will you prevent it?

lessons.title: Ethics Review Drill
lessons.objective: Evaluate an evidence plan for ethical risk and revise it.

blocks.content: Given an evidence plan, identify 3 ethical risks and propose mitigations that preserve investigative quality.
Which mitigation most improves trust without reducing effectiveness?
What additional documentation should be added for auditability?

lessons.title: Language Discipline
lessons.objective: Use neutral, precise language to prevent bias and overreach.

blocks.content: Language shapes perception. Neutral precision reduces bias and prevents narrative escalation. Replace loaded labels with observable descriptors and evidence-cited statements.
Rewrite three loaded phrases into neutral, precise statements.

lessons.title: Integrity Case Lab
lessons.objective: Apply ethical constraints to a complex scenario with competing pressures.

blocks.content: A high-profile case has intense pressure for quick answers. Build an evidence plan that preserves ethics, reduces harm, and remains bias-resistant.
Where is the biggest risk of harm and how do you reduce it?
Which step ensures fairness under uncertainty?

modules.title: Analytical Tools and Skill Habits
modules.summary: Practical tools: checklists, matrices, time windows, and structured synthesis habits.

lessons.title: Checklists as Quality Gates
lessons.objective: Use checklists to prevent avoidable reasoning errors.

blocks.content: Checklists are not bureaucracy; they are error-prevention tools. Use them at transitions: hypothesis updates, report drafts, escalation decisions, and evidence handoffs.
Create a 6-item checklist you would run before closing a case phase.

lessons.title: Evidence-Claim Matrix
lessons.objective: Organize claims and their supporting evidence to reveal gaps and overreach.

blocks.content: An evidence-claim matrix lists claims as rows and evidence items as columns. It shows which claims are weak, which are over-supported, and where corroboration is missing.
Build a matrix with 4 claims and 6 evidence items. Mark support strength and independence.
Which claim is most fragile and what would strengthen it?

lessons.title: Time Window Tables
lessons.objective: Use time window tables to prevent timeline drift and false precision.

blocks.content: Time window tables track events with min/max bounds, evidence sources, and uncertainty notes. They keep investigations honest when timestamps conflict.
Draft a time window table with 5 events for a hypothetical scenario.

lessons.title: Assumption-to-Test Lists
lessons.objective: Turn assumptions into testable questions and collection actions.

blocks.content: Each assumption should become a test: what evidence would confirm or falsify it? Assumption-to-test lists convert vague beliefs into actionable collection plans.
Assumption: 'The suspect knew the victim.' Create three tests and list evidence sources.
What makes a test discriminating rather than confirmatory?

lessons.title: Matrix Drill
lessons.objective: Practice building a claim matrix and revising claims to match evidence strength.

blocks.content: Given 6 evidence items, build 4 claims. Mark support. Downgrade any claim that is overreaching and add explicit limits.
Which claim did you downgrade and why?
What single evidence item would allow you to upgrade it again?

lessons.title: Synthesis Without Overreach
lessons.objective: Synthesize findings into a coherent picture while preserving uncertainty.

blocks.content: Synthesis should be coherent but not overconfident. Preserve uncertainty by stating what is known, what is likely, and what remains unknown.
Write a synthesis paragraph with explicit known/likely/unknown structure.

lessons.title: Learning Loop: After-Action Reviews
lessons.objective: Use after-action reviews to improve reasoning quality over time.

blocks.content: After-action reviews evaluate process: where assumptions were wrong, where bias appeared, what evidence was most discriminating, and what would be done differently next time.
Write an AAR outline for a completed case scenario.

lessons.title: Synthesis Lab
lessons.objective: Build a defensible synthesis using matrices, time windows, and limits.

blocks.content: Given a mixed evidence set, build: (1) a time window table, (2) a claim matrix, (3) a synthesis summary with explicit limits.
Where is uncertainty highest and what test would reduce it most?
Which claim is strongest and why is it strong?

modules.title: Applied Foundations Drills
modules.summary: Short applied drills that reinforce foundations in realistic micro-scenarios.

lessons.title: Micro-Scenario: Conflicting Witnesses
lessons.objective: Use evidence hierarchy and corroboration to handle conflicting accounts.

blocks.content: Two witnesses disagree on suspect clothing color. Identify what can be corroborated and what should remain uncertain.
What independent evidence would resolve the conflict?
How would you report this conflict without choosing a side?

lessons.title: Micro-Scenario: Timeline Gap
lessons.objective: Convert a timeline gap into time windows and targeted evidence tests.

blocks.content: There is a 45-minute period with no sightings. Create a time window plan and list evidence sources to tighten bounds.
Which source is most discriminating and why?
What is the highest-risk assumption in your plan?

lessons.title: Micro-Scenario: Ambiguous Digital Artifact
lessons.objective: Avoid overinterpretation of digital traces without authenticity validation.

blocks.content: A screenshot suggests a threat message, but metadata is missing. List validation steps and limits on interpretation.
What would authenticate this artifact?
How would you describe it in a report today?

lessons.title: Micro-Scenario: Scene Noise
lessons.objective: Separate context noise from signal using hypothesis relevance tests.

blocks.content: The scene contains multiple unrelated items. Identify which items might be noise and justify with relevance to hypotheses.
What evidence would prove an item is relevant?
Which hypothesis is most sensitive to this item?

lessons.title: Micro-Scenario: Premature Closure
lessons.objective: Detect premature closure and keep alternatives alive until discriminators arrive.

blocks.content: A plausible suspect emerges early. List two alternatives and define discriminating evidence to avoid premature closure.
What would change your mind about the early suspect?
What is your next evidence collection step and why?

lessons.title: Micro-Scenario: Evidence-Claim Matrix
lessons.objective: Map claims to evidence to reveal gaps and overreach.

blocks.content: Create 3 claims from 5 evidence items and build a simple claim-evidence mapping. Downgrade any claim that overreaches.
Which claim was weakest?
What evidence would most strengthen it?

lessons.title: Micro-Scenario: Ethics Constraint
lessons.objective: Apply ethics and harm reduction while preserving investigative quality.

blocks.content: A piece of evidence is sensitive and could cause harm if mishandled. Propose a plan that preserves integrity and minimizes harm.
What documentation is required?
How do you communicate uncertainty without escalation?

lessons.title: Foundations Capstone Lab
lessons.objective: Synthesize constraints, hypotheses, corroboration, and reporting into a defensible output.

blocks.content: Given a compact evidence pack, produce: (1) 3 hypotheses, (2) discriminating tests, (3) a time window table, and (4) an evidence-first summary with limits.
Where is your uncertainty highest and why?
Which test would reduce uncertainty the most quickly?
